meta.strand: forward (GRCh37). The engine auto-flips non-palindromic genotypes reported on the opposite strand.
meta.note: Positions and letters were checked against dbSNP (tools/verify_library.py). Interpretation texts have not had clinical review; markers with verify.level "inferred" are shown with a dagger.

categories.name: Carrier status (conditions you could pass on to children)

markers.name: Factor V Leiden

CC.text: No copies of Factor V Leiden, the most common inherited clotting tendency.

CT.text: One copy of Factor V Leiden, which raises clot risk several-fold. Many carriers never clot, but tell your doctor, especially before surgery, long travel, or estrogen-containing medication.

TT.text: Two copies of Factor V Leiden, which raises clot risk substantially. Discuss with a doctor.

markers.caveat: Does not rule out other clotting causes.
markers.about: Factor V is a clotting protein. The Leiden change makes it harder to switch off, so blood clots a little more easily; about 1 in 20 people of European ancestry carry one copy.

markers.name: Prothrombin G20210A

GG.text: No copies of this inherited clotting variant.

AG.text: One copy of the prothrombin variant, which modestly raises clot risk. Tell your doctor before surgery, long travel, or estrogen-containing medication.

AA.text: Two copies of the prothrombin variant, which raises clot risk. Discuss with a doctor.

markers.caveat: Does not rule out other clotting causes.
markers.about: This change raises production of prothrombin, a key clotting protein, so clots form a little more easily. About 1 in 50 people of European ancestry carry it.

markers.name: HFE C282Y

GG.text: No copies of the main hemochromatosis (iron overload) variant.

AG.text: One copy (carrier). Usually no iron overload on its own; matters mainly if paired with an H63D copy.

AA.text: Two copies of the main hemochromatosis variant. Ask a doctor about ferritin and transferrin saturation tests.

markers.caveat: Rarer iron variants are not covered.
markers.about: HFE helps the body sense its iron. C282Y breaks it, so the gut keeps absorbing iron; two copies is the main cause of hemochromatosis, though many with two copies never overload.

markers.name: HFE H63D

CC.text: No copies of H63D.

CG.text: One copy of a very common minor iron variant. Rarely matters on its own; matters mainly when paired with a C282Y copy.

GG.text: Two copies of H63D. Usually mild or no iron overload; mention it if iron tests are ever high.

markers.caveat: Common in roughly 1 in 5 people of European ancestry.
markers.about: A milder change in the same iron-sensing protein. It rarely causes iron overload unless paired with C282Y.

markers.name: HFE S65C

AA.text: No copies of this rarer iron-overload variant.

AT.text: One copy of a rare minor iron variant; rarely significant on its own.

TT.text: Two copies of a rare minor iron variant; mention to your doctor if iron tests are ever high.

markers.about: A rare, mild HFE change. Paired with C282Y it can slightly raise iron; on its own it does not cause overload.

markers.name: CYP2C9*3

AA.text: No copies of the slow-enzyme version (affects drugs such as warfarin and some NSAIDs).

AC.text: One copy of the slow-enzyme version. Some drugs (e.g., warfarin, some NSAIDs) may stay in the body longer; mention to prescribers.

CC.text: Two copies: much slower processing of some drugs (e.g., warfarin). Tell prescribers; doses may need adjusting.

markers.caveat: Only some CYP2C9 variants are covered; not a full metabolizer status.
markers.about: CYP2C9 is a liver enzyme that clears warfarin, phenytoin and some NSAIDs. The *3 version works much more slowly, so these drugs can build up.

markers.name: CYP2C9*2

CC.text: No copies of this slow-enzyme version.

CT.text: One copy of a mildly slower enzyme version; mention to prescribers of warfarin or some NSAIDs.

TT.text: Two copies: slower processing of some drugs (e.g., warfarin). Tell prescribers.

verify.note: Check coverage on 23andMe chips.

markers.about: A CYP2C9 version that works somewhat more slowly, though less so than *3. Warfarin and phenytoin guidelines account for it.

markers.name: CYP2C19*2

GG.text: No copies of the slow-enzyme version (affects clopidogrel, some antidepressants and PPIs).

AG.text: One copy of a reduced-function version. Clopidogrel may work less well and some antidepressants and PPIs may be processed more slowly; mention to prescribers.

AA.text: Two copies: poor processing of some drugs. Clopidogrel may be much less effective; tell prescribers.

markers.caveat: Other CYP2C19 variants are not all covered.
markers.about: CYP2C19 activates clopidogrel (a heart drug) and clears many antidepressants and PPIs. *2 is a non-working version and the most common cause of slow processing.

markers.name: CYP2C19*3

GG.text: No copies of this slow-enzyme version.

AG.text: One copy of a no-function version; same cautions as CYP2C19*2.

AA.text: Two copies: poor processing of some drugs; tell prescribers.

markers.about: Another non-working CYP2C19 version, with the same effect as *2. It is most common in people of East Asian ancestry.

markers.name: CYP2C19*17

CC.text: No copies of the faster-enzyme version.

CT.text: One copy of the faster-enzyme version; some drugs (some antidepressants, PPIs) may be cleared faster than average.

TT.text: Two copies: faster-than-average processing of some drugs, so standard doses may work less well.

verify.note: Check coverage on 23andMe chips.

markers.about: This change raises CYP2C19 production, so some antidepressants and PPIs are cleared faster and may work less well.

markers.name: CYP2D6*4

CC.text: No copies of this non-working enzyme version.

CT.text: One copy of a non-working version: reduced processing of many drugs (e.g., some antidepressants, codeine).

TT.text: Two copies: poor processing of many drugs (e.g., codeine may not work; some antidepressants build up). Tell prescribers.

markers.caveat: CYP2D6 has many other variants and gene copy-number changes.

verify.note: Strand verified against dbSNP; not on the AncestryDNA chip. Awaiting expert review.

markers.about: CYP2D6 processes about 1 in 4 common medicines, including codeine, tramadol, tamoxifen and many antidepressants. *4 does not work, so codeine may not relieve pain.

markers.name: CYP3A5*3

TT.text: No *3 copies: you likely make the CYP3A5 enzyme, which affects dosing of some drugs (e.g., tacrolimus).

CT.text: One copy of the common low-expresser version.

CC.text: Two copies of the common low-expresser version, typical for many people; mainly matters for dosing some transplant drugs (e.g., tacrolimus).

markers.caveat: Allele frequencies differ widely between populations.

verify.note: Normal/variant direction and strand were inferred.

markers.about: CYP3A5 helps clear the transplant drug tacrolimus. *3 switches it off and is the usual version in people of European ancestry; people who make the enzyme need higher doses.

markers.name: SLCO1B1 (statin muscle side effects)

TT.text: No copies of the version linked to statin muscle side effects.

CT.text: One copy: somewhat higher risk of muscle side effects from some statins (especially simvastatin); mention to your prescriber.

CC.text: Two copies: higher risk of statin muscle side effects; mention to your prescriber.

markers.about: SLCO1B1 pulls statins from the blood into the liver. This weaker version leaves more statin in the blood, raising the risk of muscle aches, mainly with simvastatin.

markers.name: TPMT*2

CC.text: No copies of this reduced-function TPMT variant.

CG.text: One copy: lower TPMT activity, so thiopurine drugs (azathioprine, mercaptopurine) may need lower doses.

GG.text: Two copies: very low TPMT activity; thiopurine drugs can cause serious toxicity at standard doses. Tell prescribers.

markers.caveat: Other TPMT variants are not covered.

verify.note: Strand verified against dbSNP. Awaiting expert review.

markers.about: TPMT clears thiopurine drugs (azathioprine, mercaptopurine). This weaker version lets them build up and harm the bone marrow at standard doses. *2 is rare.

markers.name: TPMT*3B

CC.text: No copies of this reduced-function TPMT variant.

CT.text: One copy: lower TPMT activity, so thiopurine drugs (azathioprine, mercaptopurine) may need lower doses.

TT.text: Two copies: very low TPMT activity; thiopurine drugs can cause serious toxicity at standard doses. Tell prescribers.

markers.caveat: Other TPMT variants are not covered.

verify.note: Strand verified against dbSNP. Awaiting expert review.

markers.about: TPMT clears thiopurine drugs (azathioprine, mercaptopurine). This weaker version lets them build up and harm the bone marrow at standard doses. *3B usually sits with *3C on the same copy, forming *3A, the most common weak version in Europeans.

markers.name: TPMT*3C

TT.text: No copies of this reduced-function TPMT variant.

CT.text: One copy: lower TPMT activity, so thiopurine drugs (azathioprine, mercaptopurine) may need lower doses.

CC.text: Two copies: very low TPMT activity; thiopurine drugs can cause serious toxicity at standard doses. Tell prescribers.

markers.caveat: Other TPMT variants are not covered.

verify.note: Strand verified against dbSNP. Awaiting expert review.

markers.about: TPMT clears thiopurine drugs (azathioprine, mercaptopurine). This weaker version lets them build up and harm the bone marrow at standard doses. With *3B it forms *3A; on its own *3C is the main weak version in East Asian and African ancestry.

markers.name: DPYD*2A (chemotherapy sensitivity)

CC.text: No copies of this chemotherapy-sensitivity variant.

CT.text: One copy: higher risk of severe toxicity from fluoropyrimidine chemotherapy (5-FU, capecitabine). Tell your oncologist if you ever need these drugs.

TT.text: Two copies: very high risk of severe toxicity from fluoropyrimidine chemotherapy. Tell your doctors.

markers.caveat: Other DPYD variants are not covered.
markers.about: DPYD breaks down the chemotherapy drugs 5-FU and capecitabine. *2A does not work, so standard doses can cause severe side effects; guidelines lower the starting dose.

markers.name: HLA-B*57:01 proxy (abacavir hypersensitivity)

TT.text: The proxy marker shows no sign of the abacavir (HIV drug) hypersensitivity gene.

GT.text: The proxy marker suggests HLA-B*57:01 may be present, which can cause a serious reaction to abacavir. A clinical HLA test is needed; tell prescribers.

GG.text: The proxy marker suggests two HLA-B*57:01 copies. A clinical HLA test is needed; tell prescribers.

markers.caveat: A proxy only; a clinical HLA test is required before prescribing abacavir.

verify.note: Proxy accuracy varies by ancestry.

markers.about: HLA-B*57:01 can cause a serious allergic reaction to abacavir, an HIV drug. This marker usually travels with it, but a direct HLA test is done before prescribing.

markers.name: OPRM1 (opioid response)

AA.text: The most common version; no copies of the variant sometimes linked to needing higher opioid doses.

AG.text: One copy of a variant sometimes linked to needing slightly higher opioid doses.

GG.text: Two copies of a variant sometimes linked to needing higher opioid doses. Evidence is weak.

markers.caveat: Evidence is weak.
markers.about: OPRM1 is the main receptor opioid painkillers act on. Large studies disagree on this variant, and guidelines advise against using it to change doses.

markers.name: MTHFR C677T

GG.text: No copies of the variant.

AG.text: One copy: folate (a B vitamin) is processed slightly slower. Typically no real health effect.

AA.text: Two copies: about 65% reduced enzyme activity; may mildly raise homocysteine, especially with low folate. Ask your doctor if relevant.

markers.caveat: Not treated as a medical issue by itself; be wary of supplement marketing.

verify.note: Reported on the coding (C/T) strand by some sources; the engine auto-flips.

markers.about: MTHFR activates folate. C677T makes the enzyme less stable, mainly when folate is low; medical groups advise against testing or treating it on its own.

markers.name: MTHFR A1298C

TT.text: No copies of the second MTHFR variant.

GT.text: One copy of the second MTHFR variant; typically no health effect.

GG.text: Two copies of the second MTHFR variant; small effect on folate processing.

markers.about: A second, milder MTHFR change with little or no effect on its own.

markers.name: COMT Val158Met

GG.text: Two copies of the "Val" version (faster dopamine clearance).

AG.text: One of each version.

AA.text: Two copies of the "Met" version (slower dopamine clearance, nicknamed "worrier gene"). Research is weak and inconsistent; it does not predict anxiety or personality.

markers.caveat: Weak evidence; not predictive.
markers.about: COMT breaks down dopamine in the front of the brain; the Met version is less active. Large studies have not found it predicts personality or stress handling.

markers.name: Heart disease, 9p21 region (marker 1)

GG.text: No copies of the risk version of a well-known heart disease marker. Lower end of genetic risk.

CG.text: One copy of the risk version; a small increase in heart disease risk.

CC.text: Two copies of the risk version; modestly higher heart disease risk. Lifestyle and family history matter more.

markers.caveat: Small effect even in carriers.
markers.about: This chromosome 9 region is the strongest common genetic signal for heart disease. Each risk copy raises risk by about a quarter, less than smoking, blood pressure or cholesterol.

markers.name: Heart disease, 9p21 region (marker 2)

AA.text: No copies of the risk version (agrees with marker 1 if both are present).

AG.text: One copy of the risk version; a small increase in heart disease risk.

GG.text: Two copies of the risk version; modestly higher heart disease risk.

markers.caveat: Small effect even in carriers.
markers.about: A second marker in the same 9p21 heart region. It usually travels with the first, so the two give one signal, not double the risk.

markers.name: Lipoprotein(a), LPA variant 1

AA.text: No copies of this variant linked to higher lipoprotein(a).

AG.text: One copy of a variant linked to higher lipoprotein(a) (Lp(a)), a mostly inherited heart disease risk factor that diet barely changes. Consider asking your doctor about a one-time Lp(a) blood test.

GG.text: Two copies of a variant linked to much higher Lp(a). Ask your doctor about an Lp(a) blood test.

markers.caveat: The blood level is more informative than the variant.
markers.about: LPA makes lipoprotein(a), a cholesterol particle that promotes plaque and clotting. Lp(a) is mostly set by genes, and this is one of its strongest common markers.

markers.name: Lipoprotein(a), LPA variant 2

TT.text: No copies of this second Lp(a)-raising variant.

CT.text: One copy of a variant linked to higher Lp(a). Consider asking about an Lp(a) blood test.

CC.text: Two copies of a variant linked to higher Lp(a). Ask your doctor about an Lp(a) blood test.

markers.caveat: The blood level is more informative than the variant.
markers.about: A second, less common LPA variant linked to high Lp(a). A one-time Lp(a) blood test shows your actual level.

markers.name: APOB R3527Q

CC.text: No copies of this inherited high-cholesterol variant.

CT.text: One copy of a variant that can cause inherited high LDL cholesterol (familial defective apoB). Ask your doctor about lipid testing.

TT.text: Two copies; ask your doctor about lipid testing and treatment.

markers.caveat: Many other familial hypercholesterolemia variants are not covered.
markers.about: APOB lets the liver pull LDL cholesterol out of the blood. R3527Q weakens that grip, causing a form of inherited high cholesterol that responds well to treatment.

markers.name: PCSK9 R46L

GG.text: No copies of the variant linked to lower LDL cholesterol (neither a benefit nor a risk).

GT.text: One copy of a variant linked to lower LDL cholesterol and lower heart disease risk.

TT.text: Two copies of a variant linked to much lower LDL cholesterol.

markers.about: PCSK9 destroys the liver's LDL receptors. R46L weakens it, giving lower LDL and heart risk; findings like this led to PCSK9-blocking drugs.

markers.name: Atrial fibrillation, 4q25 region

GG.text: No copies of this common AFib-linked variant.

GT.text: One copy of a common variant linked to a modestly higher risk of atrial fibrillation. One common variant explains very little.

TT.text: Two copies of a common AFib-linked variant; modestly higher risk. Mention family history of AFib to your doctor.

markers.caveat: The strongest marker in this region (rs2200733) is not on AncestryDNA arrays.
markers.about: This region near PITX2 is the strongest common genetic signal for atrial fibrillation. Each risk copy raises risk modestly; age, blood pressure and alcohol matter more.

markers.name: Atrial fibrillation, KCNN3

CC.text: No copies of the risk version of this common AFib marker.

CT.text: One copy of a common AFib-linked variant; small effect.

TT.text: Two copies of a common AFib-linked variant; modest effect.

verify.note: Risk-allele direction from published studies. Awaiting expert review.

markers.about: KCNN3 helps heart cells reset after each beat. This common variant slightly raises the chance of atrial fibrillation.

markers.name: Type 2 diabetes, TCF7L2

CC.text: No copies of the risk version of the strongest common diabetes marker. Lower end of genetic risk.

CT.text: One copy of the risk version; a modest increase in type 2 diabetes risk.

TT.text: Two copies of the risk version; a moderate increase in type 2 diabetes risk. Weight, diet and activity matter much more.

markers.caveat: Lifestyle matters more than any one gene.
markers.about: TCF7L2 helps control insulin release. This is the strongest common genetic risk factor for type 2 diabetes (about 40% per copy), but weight, activity and diet matter more.

markers.name: Type 2 diabetes, KCNJ11

CC.text: No copies of the risk version.

CT.text: One copy of a common version with a very small effect on type 2 diabetes risk.

TT.text: Two copies of a common version with a small effect on type 2 diabetes risk.

markers.about: KCNJ11 is part of the channel that triggers insulin release. This version makes it slightly less responsive, raising type 2 diabetes risk by about 15% per copy.

markers.name: Type 2 diabetes, PPARG

CC.text: No copies of the "Ala" version: the usual Pro/Pro type.

CG.text: One copy of the "Ala" version, which is very slightly protective against type 2 diabetes.

GG.text: Two copies of the "Ala" version, which is slightly protective against type 2 diabetes.

markers.caveat: Small effect.
markers.about: PPARG controls how fat cells respond to insulin. The common Pro version carries slightly higher type 2 diabetes risk; Ala lowers it somewhat.

markers.name: Type 2 diabetes, SLC30A8

TT.text: No copies of the slightly higher-risk version.

CT.text: One copy of a common version with a very small effect on type 2 diabetes risk.

CC.text: Two copies of the more common version with a very small effect on diabetes risk. Most people have at least one.

markers.about: SLC30A8 is a zinc transporter that helps the pancreas store insulin. The common version slightly raises type 2 diabetes risk.

markers.name: Blood sugar, MTNR1B

CC.text: No copies of the variant linked to higher fasting blood sugar.

CG.text: One copy of a version linked to slightly higher fasting blood sugar. Small effect.

GG.text: Two copies of a version linked to higher fasting blood sugar. Small to modest effect.

markers.about: MTNR1B is a melatonin receptor on insulin-making cells. This variant dampens insulin release and is linked to higher fasting sugar and type 2 diabetes risk.

markers.name: Weight tendency, FTO

TT.text: No copies of the version linked to a small weight gain tendency.

AT.text: One copy of a version linked to a small weight gain tendency.

AA.text: Two copies of a version linked to a modest weight gain tendency. Diet and activity matter much more.

verify.note: A/T marker: strand cannot be auto-checked.

markers.about: FTO has the strongest common link to body weight. Each risk copy is tied to more appetite and about 1 to 1.5 kg (2 to 3 lb); regular activity weakens the effect.

markers.name: Weight tendency, MC4R

TT.text: No copies of the MC4R version linked to slightly higher weight.

CT.text: One copy of a common MC4R version linked to slightly higher weight, under a kilogram (1 to 2 pounds) on average. Diet and activity matter much more.

CC.text: Two copies of a common MC4R version linked to slightly higher weight, about 1 to 2 kilograms (2 to 4 pounds) on average. Diet and activity matter much more.

markers.caveat: Small effect; it does not predict your weight.

verify.note: Risk allele C per Loos 2008; forward-strand letters checked against dbSNP.

markers.about: MC4R is a brain receptor that signals fullness. This common variant slightly weakens it, adding on average a fraction of a kilogram.

markers.name: Colorectal cancer, 8q24 region

TT.text: No copies of the version linked to a slightly higher colorectal cancer risk.

GT.text: One copy of a version linked to a slightly higher colorectal cancer risk (small effect). Does not change screening advice beyond family-history guidance.

GG.text: Two copies of a version linked to a slightly higher colorectal cancer risk (small effect). Does not change screening advice beyond family-history guidance.

markers.caveat: Common, low-impact variant.

verify.note: Risk-allele direction from published studies. Awaiting expert review.

markers.about: This chromosome 8 region controls MYC, a cell-growth gene. The risk version raises colorectal cancer risk by about 20% per copy; screening matters far more.

markers.name: Stomach cancer, PSCA

CC.text: No copies of the version linked to slightly higher stomach cancer risk.

CT.text: One copy of a common version linked to slightly higher stomach cancer risk in some studies (small effect).

TT.text: Two copies of a common version linked to slightly higher stomach cancer risk in some studies (small effect).

markers.caveat: Low-impact variant.

verify.note: Risk-allele direction from published studies. Awaiting expert review.

markers.about: PSCA is a stomach-lining protein. This variant is linked to higher stomach and bladder cancer risk, mostly studied in East Asia; H. pylori matters much more.

markers.name: BRCA1 5382insC

DD.text: No copies of the BRCA1 5382insC variant.

DI.text: One copy of the BRCA1 5382insC variant (breast and ovarian cancer predisposition). This is a screening-grade result: confirm with clinical testing and talk with a doctor or genetic counselor.

II.text: Two copies of the BRCA1 5382insC variant (breast and ovarian cancer predisposition). Confirm with clinical testing and talk with a doctor or genetic counselor.

markers.caveat: Checks only 1 of thousands of BRCA variants. If family history exists, ask about clinical testing.

verify.note: D/I notation: normal = DD assumed; check vendor documentation.

markers.about: BRCA1 repairs broken DNA. 5382insC breaks it and is one of three Ashkenazi Jewish founder variants that sharply raise breast and ovarian cancer risk.

markers.name: BRCA2 6174delT

II.text: No copies of the BRCA2 6174delT variant.

DI.text: One copy of the BRCA2 6174delT variant (breast, ovarian, prostate and pancreatic cancer predisposition). This is a screening-grade result: confirm with clinical testing and talk with a doctor or genetic counselor.

DD.text: Two copies of the BRCA2 6174delT variant (breast, ovarian, prostate and pancreatic cancer predisposition). Confirm with clinical testing and talk with a doctor or genetic counselor.

markers.caveat: Checks only 1 of thousands of BRCA variants. If family history exists, ask about clinical testing.

verify.note: D/I notation: normal = II assumed; check vendor documentation.

markers.about: The third Ashkenazi Jewish founder variant, in the DNA-repair gene BRCA2. It raises breast, ovarian, prostate and pancreatic cancer risk.

markers.name: CHEK2 1100delC

II.text: No copies of the CHEK2 1100delC variant.

DI.text: One copy of the CHEK2 1100delC variant (breast and other cancer predisposition). This is a screening-grade result: confirm with clinical testing and talk with a doctor or genetic counselor.

DD.text: Two copies of the CHEK2 1100delC variant (breast and other cancer predisposition). Confirm with clinical testing and talk with a doctor or genetic counselor.

markers.caveat: Many other CHEK2 variants are not covered.

verify.note: D/I notation: normal = II assumed.

markers.about: CHEK2 pauses cell division when DNA is damaged. 1100delC breaks it and roughly doubles breast cancer risk; screening guidelines exist for carriers.

markers.name: MUTYH G396D

CC.text: No copies of the MUTYH G396D variant.

CT.text: One copy of the MUTYH G396D variant (colorectal cancer predisposition; two copies cause MUTYH-associated polyposis). This is a screening-grade result: confirm with clinical testing and talk with a doctor or genetic counselor.

TT.text: Two copies of the MUTYH G396D variant (colorectal cancer predisposition; two copies cause MUTYH-associated polyposis). Confirm with clinical testing and talk with a doctor or genetic counselor.

markers.caveat: Other MUTYH variants are not covered.
markers.about: MUTYH repairs one kind of DNA damage. G396D is a common harmful variant; two harmful copies cause many colon polyps, one has at most a small effect.

markers.name: MUTYH Y179C

TT.text: No copies of the MUTYH Y179C variant.

CT.text: One copy of the MUTYH Y179C variant (colorectal cancer predisposition; two copies cause MUTYH-associated polyposis). This is a screening-grade result: confirm with clinical testing and talk with a doctor or genetic counselor.

CC.text: Two copies of the MUTYH Y179C variant (colorectal cancer predisposition; two copies cause MUTYH-associated polyposis). Confirm with clinical testing and talk with a doctor or genetic counselor.

markers.caveat: Other MUTYH variants are not covered.
markers.about: The other common harmful MUTYH variant. Two harmful copies of either kind cause MUTYH polyposis; one copy makes you a carrier.

markers.name: APC I1307K

TT.text: No copies of the APC I1307K variant.

AT.text: One copy of the APC I1307K variant (higher colorectal cancer risk). This is a screening-grade result: confirm with clinical testing and talk with a doctor or genetic counselor.

AA.text: Two copies of the APC I1307K variant (higher colorectal cancer risk). Confirm with clinical testing and talk with a doctor or genetic counselor.

markers.about: APC keeps gut-lining growth in check. I1307K raises colorectal cancer risk about 1.5 to 2 times; about 6% of Ashkenazi Jews carry it and are often advised earlier colonoscopy.

markers.name: HOXB13 G84E

CC.text: No copies of the HOXB13 G84E variant.

CT.text: One copy of the HOXB13 G84E variant (higher prostate cancer risk). This is a screening-grade result: confirm with clinical testing and talk with a doctor or genetic counselor.

TT.text: Two copies of the HOXB13 G84E variant (higher prostate cancer risk). Confirm with clinical testing and talk with a doctor or genetic counselor.

markers.about: HOXB13 guides prostate development. G84E, mostly in Northern Europeans, raises prostate cancer risk several times and is linked to earlier onset.

markers.name: TP53 R337H

CC.text: No copies of the TP53 R337H variant.

CT.text: One copy of the TP53 R337H variant (Li-Fraumeni-type cancer predisposition). This is a screening-grade result: confirm with clinical testing and talk with a doctor or genetic counselor.

TT.text: Two copies of the TP53 R337H variant (Li-Fraumeni-type cancer predisposition). Confirm with clinical testing and talk with a doctor or genetic counselor.

markers.about: TP53 is the main tumor-suppressor gene. R337H, common in southern Brazil, causes a milder Li-Fraumeni syndrome; elsewhere it is very rare and chip calls are often wrong.

markers.name: TREM2 R47H

CC.text: No copies of the TREM2 R47H variant.

CT.text: One copy of the TREM2 R47H variant (higher Alzheimer's risk). This is a screening-grade result: confirm with clinical testing and talk with a doctor or genetic counselor.

TT.text: Two copies of the TREM2 R47H variant (higher Alzheimer's risk). Confirm with clinical testing and talk with a doctor or genetic counselor.

markers.about: TREM2 helps brain immune cells clear debris such as amyloid. The rare R47H weakens this and raises Alzheimer's risk about two to three times.

markers.name: LRRK2 G2019S

GG.text: No copies of the LRRK2 G2019S variant.

AG.text: One copy of the LRRK2 G2019S variant (inherited Parkinson's risk). This is a screening-grade result: confirm with clinical testing and talk with a doctor or genetic counselor.

AA.text: Two copies of the LRRK2 G2019S variant (inherited Parkinson's risk). Confirm with clinical testing and talk with a doctor or genetic counselor.

markers.about: G2019S makes LRRK2 overactive and is the most common known genetic cause of Parkinson's, but most carriers never develop it (lifetime risk about 25 to 40%).

markers.name: GBA N370S

TT.text: No copies of the GBA N370S variant.

CT.text: One copy: carrier of the Gaucher disease variant, which also modestly raises Parkinson's risk.

CC.text: Two copies: Gaucher disease. See a doctor.

verify.note: Strand verified against dbSNP; not on the AncestryDNA chip. Awaiting expert review.

markers.about: GBA1 breaks down a fatty substance in cells. Two N370S copies cause Gaucher disease type 1, often mild and treatable; one copy raises Parkinson's risk a few times.

markers.name: SNCA

AA.text: No copies of the version with a small effect on Parkinson's risk.

AG.text: One copy of a common version with a small effect on Parkinson's risk. About half of people carry at least one.

GG.text: Two copies of a common version with a small effect on Parkinson's risk.

markers.caveat: Small effect.
markers.about: SNCA makes alpha-synuclein, the protein that clumps in Parkinson's. This common variant raises Parkinson's risk by about 30% per copy, a small effect.

markers.name: CFTR G542X

GG.text: No copies of the CFTR G542X variant.

GT.text: One copy of the CFTR G542X variant (cystic fibrosis carrier status). Carriers usually have no symptoms but can pass it on, which matters for family planning. Confirm clinically.

TT.text: Two copies of the CFTR G542X variant (cystic fibrosis). Two copies can mean you have the condition itself, not just carrier status. See a doctor or genetic counselor and confirm with clinical testing.

markers.caveat: Many other CFTR variants exist; a carrier panel is needed if planning children.
markers.about: CFTR moves salt and water in the lungs and gut; cystic fibrosis needs both copies harmful. G542X stops the protein being made, so it is severe.

markers.name: CFTR G551D

GG.text: No copies of the CFTR G551D variant.

AG.text: One copy of the CFTR G551D variant (cystic fibrosis carrier status). Carriers usually have no symptoms but can pass it on, which matters for family planning. Confirm clinically.

AA.text: Two copies of the CFTR G551D variant (cystic fibrosis). Two copies can mean you have the condition itself, not just carrier status. See a doctor or genetic counselor and confirm with clinical testing.

markers.caveat: Many other CFTR variants exist; a carrier panel is needed if planning children.
markers.about: CFTR moves salt and water in the lungs and gut; cystic fibrosis needs both copies harmful. G551D makes a channel that will not open; it was the first treated by ivacaftor.

markers.name: CFTR W1282X

GG.text: No copies of the CFTR W1282X variant.

AG.text: One copy of the CFTR W1282X variant (cystic fibrosis carrier status). Carriers usually have no symptoms but can pass it on, which matters for family planning. Confirm clinically.

AA.text: Two copies of the CFTR W1282X variant (cystic fibrosis). Two copies can mean you have the condition itself, not just carrier status. See a doctor or genetic counselor and confirm with clinical testing.

markers.caveat: Many other CFTR variants exist; a carrier panel is needed if planning children.
markers.about: CFTR moves salt and water in the lungs and gut; cystic fibrosis needs both copies harmful. W1282X stops the protein early and is the most common CF variant in Ashkenazi Jews.

markers.name: CFTR R117H

GG.text: No copies of the CFTR R117H variant.

AG.text: One copy of the CFTR R117H variant (cystic fibrosis carrier status). Carriers usually have no symptoms but can pass it on, which matters for family planning. Confirm clinically.

AA.text: Two copies of the CFTR R117H variant (cystic fibrosis). Two copies can mean you have the condition itself, not just carrier status. See a doctor or genetic counselor and confirm with clinical testing.

markers.caveat: Many other CFTR variants exist; a carrier panel is needed if planning children.
markers.about: CFTR moves salt and water in the lungs and gut; cystic fibrosis needs both copies harmful. R117H leaves the channel partly working, so it is mild, from no symptoms to mild CF.

markers.name: CFTR F508del

II.text: No copies of the CFTR F508del variant.

DI.text: One copy of the CFTR F508del variant (cystic fibrosis carrier status). Carriers usually have no symptoms but can pass it on, which matters for family planning. Confirm clinically.

DD.text: Two copies of the CFTR F508del variant (cystic fibrosis). Two copies can mean you have the condition itself, not just carrier status. See a doctor or genetic counselor and confirm with clinical testing.

markers.caveat: Many other CFTR variants exist; a carrier panel is needed if planning children.

verify.note: D/I notation: normal = II assumed.

markers.about: CFTR moves salt and water in the lungs and gut; cystic fibrosis needs both copies harmful. F508del makes the channel misfold and is behind about 70% of CF copies in Europeans.

markers.name: GJB2 35delG

II.text: No copies of the GJB2 35delG variant.

DI.text: One copy of the GJB2 35delG variant (hearing loss carrier status). Carriers usually have no symptoms but can pass it on, which matters for family planning. Confirm clinically.

DD.text: Two copies of the GJB2 35delG variant (hearing loss). Two copies can mean you have the condition itself, not just carrier status. See a doctor or genetic counselor and confirm with clinical testing.

verify.note: D/I notation: normal = II assumed.

markers.about: GJB2 makes connexin 26, needed for hearing. 35delG is the most common cause of inherited hearing loss in Europeans; two copies usually cause it, one makes you a carrier.

markers.name: Hemoglobin C (HBB)

CC.text: No copies of the Hemoglobin C (HBB) variant.

CT.text: One copy of the Hemoglobin C (HBB) variant (hemoglobin C carrier status). Carriers usually have no symptoms but can pass it on, which matters for family planning. Confirm clinically.

TT.text: Two copies of the Hemoglobin C (HBB) variant (hemoglobin C). Two copies can mean you have the condition itself, not just carrier status. See a doctor or genetic counselor and confirm with clinical testing.

markers.about: Hemoglobin C, common in West African ancestry, causes no illness with one copy and mild anemia with two; with a sickle copy it causes HbSC disease.

markers.name: Sickle cell (HBB)

TT.text: No copies of the sickle cell variant.

AT.text: One copy: sickle cell trait. Usually no symptoms, but can matter with extreme exertion or high altitude, and for family planning.

AA.text: Two copies: sickle cell disease. See a doctor.

verify.note: Strand verified against dbSNP; not on the AncestryDNA chip. Awaiting expert review.

markers.about: HBB makes part of hemoglobin. One sickle copy (trait) is usually harmless and protects against malaria; two copies cause sickle cell disease.

markers.name: G6PD deficiency (A-)

CC.text: No G6PD deficiency variant (X-linked).

CT.text: One copy (X-linked): carrier. Some drugs and foods (e.g., fava beans, certain antimalarials) can trigger anemia; mention to your doctor.

TT.text: G6PD deficiency variant present. Some drugs and foods (e.g., fava beans, certain antimalarials) can trigger anemia; tell your doctor.

markers.caveat: X-linked: males have one copy; a single variant letter in a male indicates the variant.
markers.about: G6PD protects red blood cells. With the A- version, some drugs, fava beans or infections can break red cells down; it is X-linked, so mostly affects males.

markers.name: Alpha-1 antitrypsin Z

CC.text: No copies of the Z variant.

CT.text: One copy of the Z variant: carrier; can modestly raise lung and liver disease risk, especially with smoking.

TT.text: Two copies: alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. See a doctor.

markers.about: SERPINA1 makes alpha-1 antitrypsin, which protects the lungs. Z gets stuck in the liver; two Z copies can damage lungs and liver, one only slightly raises risk.

markers.name: Alpha-1 antitrypsin S

TT.text: No copies of the S variant.

AT.text: One copy of the milder S variant; usually no problems.

AA.text: Two copies of the S variant; usually mild.

markers.about: The S version of alpha-1 antitrypsin is mildly reduced. It rarely causes problems unless paired with a Z copy, especially in smokers.

markers.name: NOD2 (Crohn's disease)

GG.text: No copies of this Crohn's disease variant.

CG.text: One copy of a variant linked to a higher risk of Crohn's disease; most carriers never develop it.

CC.text: Two copies of a variant linked to a substantially higher risk of Crohn's disease. Mention to your doctor if you have digestive symptoms.

markers.about: NOD2 helps gut immune cells recognize bacteria. G908R is one of three main NOD2 Crohn's variants; one copy raises a low risk a little.

markers.name: Macular degeneration, CFH Y402H

TT.text: No copies of the CFH risk version.

CT.text: One copy of a common version linked to higher risk of age-related macular degeneration. Absolute risk is still low; smoking and age matter most. Not smoking and regular eye exams are the main protections.

CC.text: Two copies of a version linked to a notably higher risk of macular degeneration. Not smoking and regular eye exams matter.

markers.about: CFH is a brake on part of the immune system. Y402H weakens it in the eye and is a major risk factor for macular degeneration; not smoking and a good diet help.

markers.name: Macular degeneration, ARMS2

GG.text: No copies of the second macular degeneration risk version.

GT.text: One copy of a version linked to higher macular degeneration risk; not smoking and regular eye exams help.

TT.text: Two copies of a version linked to notably higher macular degeneration risk; not smoking and regular eye exams matter.

markers.about: ARMS2 sits in the chromosome 10 region that, with CFH, carries the biggest genetic risk for macular degeneration.

markers.name: Celiac disease, HLA-DQ2.5 marker

CC.text: No copies of this celiac-permissive version.

CT.text: One copy of a celiac-permissive gene version. Roughly 1 in 3 people carry it and only a small fraction ever develop celiac. A weak predictor on its own.

TT.text: Two copies of a celiac-permissive version; higher but still small chance of celiac.

markers.caveat: Tag marker; not a diagnosis.

verify.note: Tag-SNP accuracy varies by ancestry.

markers.about: Almost everyone with celiac disease has HLA-DQ2.5 or DQ8, so having neither nearly rules it out. About 1 in 3 people have one, and few get celiac.

markers.name: Celiac disease, HLA-DQ8 marker

TT.text: No copies of the second celiac-permissive version.

CT.text: One copy of a celiac-permissive version; a weak predictor on its own.

CC.text: Two copies of a celiac-permissive version; a weak predictor on its own.

markers.caveat: Tag marker; not a diagnosis.

verify.note: Tag-SNP accuracy varies by ancestry.

markers.about: This marker tags HLA-DQ8, the second celiac-linked immune type: needed for celiac but far from enough.

markers.name: Gout, ABCG2

GG.text: No copies of the common gout risk variant.

GT.text: One copy of a common variant that raises uric acid and gout risk somewhat. Limiting alcohol (especially beer) and sugary drinks helps; mention it to a doctor if you ever have sudden joint pain attacks.

TT.text: Two copies; a higher risk of gout. Limiting alcohol and sugary drinks helps; mention to a doctor if you ever have sudden joint pain attacks.

markers.about: ABCG2 removes uric acid. This version works about half as well, raising gout risk (common in East Asia), and also raises rosuvastatin levels.

markers.name: Nicotine dependence, CHRNA5

GG.text: No copies of the variant linked to heavier nicotine dependence.

AG.text: One copy of a variant linked to heavier nicotine dependence and higher lung cancer risk in people who smoke. Mostly relevant only if you use nicotine.

AA.text: Two copies; stronger nicotine dependence and higher lung cancer risk in people who smoke. Mostly relevant only if you use nicotine; help quitting is available.

markers.about: CHRNA5 is part of a nicotine receptor. Carriers who smoke tend to smoke more, quit less easily and have higher lung cancer risk; no effect if you never smoke.

markers.name: Restless legs, BTBD9

GG.text: No copies of the risk version; lower end of genetic risk for restless legs syndrome (small effect).

AG.text: One copy of the risk version; modestly higher restless legs risk.

AA.text: Two copies of the risk version; higher restless legs risk.

markers.caveat: Small effect.

verify.note: Risk-allele direction from published studies. Awaiting expert review.

markers.about: BTBD9 is linked to restless legs, possibly through brain iron. This variant modestly raises the odds; low iron is a common, treatable contributor.

markers.name: Vitamin D, GC

TT.text: No copies of the variant linked to slightly lower vitamin D levels.

GT.text: One copy of a variant linked to slightly lower vitamin D levels. Sun, diet and supplements matter much more.

GG.text: Two copies; slightly lower vitamin D levels. Sun, diet and supplements matter much more.

markers.caveat: Small effect.

verify.note: Strand verified against dbSNP; effect direction from published studies. Awaiting expert review.

markers.about: GC carries vitamin D in the blood. This variant is linked to lower levels, but sun, diet and supplements matter more; only a blood test shows your level.

markers.name: Longevity, FOXO3

TT.text: No copies of the version weakly linked to longer life.

GT.text: One copy of a version weakly linked to longer life in several studies. Very small effect.

GG.text: Two copies of a version weakly linked to longer life. Very small effect; lifestyle dominates.

markers.caveat: Very small effect.

verify.note: Effect direction from published studies. Awaiting expert review.

markers.about: FOXO3 helps cells handle stress. This version is linked to reaching very old age in several populations, but the effect is small.

markers.name: Duffy Fya/Fyb

AA.text: Two copies of one common Duffy variant (Fyb).

AG.text: One of each common Duffy variant. With no Duffy-null copy you most likely express both. Matters mainly for transfusion matching.

GG.text: Two copies of the other common Duffy variant (Fya).

markers.caveat: Curiosity-level; transfusion matching uses lab typing.

verify.note: Allele-to-antigen mapping awaiting expert review.

markers.about: This change in the Duffy gene sets the Fy(a) or Fy(b) blood type, which matters mainly for transfusion matching and some pregnancies.

markers.name: Alcohol flush, ALDH2

GG.text: No copies of the flush variant: normal alcohol breakdown for this gene.

AG.text: One copy: alcohol flushing and a higher esophageal cancer risk with regular heavy drinking.

AA.text: Two copies: strong alcohol flush reaction and poor alcohol tolerance; heavy drinking carries a notably higher esophageal cancer risk.

markers.caveat: Most common in people of East Asian ancestry.
markers.about: ALDH2 clears acetaldehyde, the toxic product of alcohol. This version nearly switches it off, causing flushing; carriers who drink regularly have much higher esophageal cancer risk.

markers.name: Alcohol metabolism, ADH1B

CC.text: No copies of the fast-alcohol-metabolism version.

CT.text: One copy of a faster alcohol-metabolizing version, linked to a stronger reaction to alcohol and slightly lower risk of alcohol dependence.

TT.text: Two copies of the faster version; stronger reaction to alcohol and lower risk of alcohol dependence.

markers.caveat: Mostly relevant in people of East Asian ancestry.

verify.note: Effect direction from published studies. Awaiting expert review.

markers.about: This fast ADH1B version turns alcohol into acetaldehyde quickly, making drinking less pleasant and lowering the risk of alcohol dependence.

markers.name: Lactose digestion, LCT/MCM6

GG.text: No copies of the lactase-persistence version: you may lose the ability to digest lactose in adulthood (common worldwide).

AG.text: One copy of the lactase-persistence version: likely digests dairy fine as an adult.

AA.text: Two copies of the lactase-persistence version: likely digests dairy fine as an adult.

markers.caveat: Other lactase-persistence versions are read in "Lactose digestion, all versions together".
markers.about: This switch keeps lactase, the milk-sugar enzyme, on in adults and is common in Europeans. African and Middle Eastern switches are in the combined line.

markers.name: VKORC1 (warfarin sensitivity)

CC.text: No copies of the version linked to higher warfarin sensitivity.

CT.text: One copy: warfarin often needs a lower dose. Tell prescribers.

TT.text: Two copies: warfarin typically needs a much lower dose. Tell prescribers.

verify.note: Strand verified against dbSNP; not on the AncestryDNA chip. Awaiting expert review.

markers.about: VKORC1 is what warfarin blocks. This variant lowers VKORC1 production, so less warfarin is needed; it is the biggest single genetic factor in warfarin dosing.

markers.name: DPYD c.2846A>T (chemotherapy sensitivity)

TT.text: No copies of this DPYD variant.

AT.text: One copy of a reduced-function DPYD version. If you ever need 5-FU or capecitabine chemotherapy, guidelines recommend starting at about half the usual dose. Tell your oncologist.

AA.text: Two copies of a reduced-function DPYD version. 5-FU and capecitabine can be dangerous at standard doses; guidelines recommend at least halving the dose, or a different drug. Tell your doctors.

markers.caveat: Other DPYD variants are not covered.
markers.about: This weaker DPYD version slows breakdown of 5-FU and capecitabine, so standard doses can cause severe side effects. Guidelines act on it.

markers.name: DPYD HapB3 (chemotherapy sensitivity)

CC.text: No copies of DPYD HapB3.

CT.text: One copy of DPYD HapB3, a reduced-function version carried by about 1 in 20 people of European ancestry. If you ever need 5-FU or capecitabine chemotherapy, guidelines recommend starting at about half the usual dose. Tell your oncologist.

TT.text: Two copies of DPYD HapB3. 5-FU and capecitabine can be dangerous at standard doses; guidelines recommend at least halving the dose, or a different drug. Tell your doctors.

markers.caveat: This marker (c.1236G>A) stands in for the HapB3 group of changes, which almost always travel together.
markers.about: HapB3 is a group of DPYD changes that weaken the enzyme for 5-FU and capecitabine. It is the most common guideline DPYD variant in Europeans.

markers.name: UGT1A1*6 (bilirubin and some drugs)

GG.text: No copies of UGT1A1*6.

AG.text: One copy of UGT1A1*6, a slower version common in people of East Asian ancestry. Bilirubin may run slightly high. See "UGT1A1 type" below.

AA.text: Two copies of UGT1A1*6: slower clearance of bilirubin and of the cancer drug irinotecan. See "UGT1A1 type" below.

markers.about: A slower UGT1A1 version, the main one in East Asian ancestry, where *28 is less common.

markers.name: CYP2D6 100C>T (part of *10 and *4)

GG.text: No copies of this CYP2D6 change.

AG.text: One copy of a CYP2D6 change that is part of the reduced-function *10 version (common in people of East Asian ancestry) and also of the non-working *4. See "CYP2D6 type" for what it likely means.

AA.text: Two copies of a CYP2D6 change that is part of *10 and *4. See "CYP2D6 type" for what it likely means.

markers.caveat: Read together with *4 in the CYP2D6 type line.
markers.about: This CYP2D6 change is part of *10, a weaker version common in East Asian ancestry, and of *4, which does not work. Reading it with *4 tells them apart.

markers.name: CYP2D6*17

GG.text: No copies of CYP2D6*17.

AG.text: One copy of CYP2D6*17, a reduced-function version common in people of African ancestry. Some drugs, such as codeine and some antidepressants, may be processed more slowly.

AA.text: Two copies of CYP2D6*17: reduced processing of many drugs, such as codeine and some antidepressants. Mention to prescribers.

markers.about: A CYP2D6 version that works less well than usual, common in people of African ancestry.

markers.name: CYP2D6*41

CC.text: No copies of CYP2D6*41.

CT.text: One copy of CYP2D6*41, a reduced-function version carried by about 1 in 6 people of European ancestry. Some drugs may be processed more slowly.

TT.text: Two copies of CYP2D6*41: reduced processing of many drugs, such as codeine and some antidepressants. Mention to prescribers.

markers.about: A CYP2D6 version that makes less working enzyme; the most common reduced one in Europeans.

markers.name: CYP2C9*5

CC.text: No copies of CYP2C9*5.

CG.text: One copy of CYP2C9*5, a non-working version found mainly in people of African ancestry. Warfarin, phenytoin and some NSAIDs may stay in the body longer; see "CYP2C9 type".

GG.text: Two copies of CYP2C9*5: much slower processing of warfarin, phenytoin and some NSAIDs. Tell prescribers.

markers.about: A CYP2C9 version that barely works, found mainly in people of African ancestry.

markers.name: CYP2C9*8

GG.text: No copies of CYP2C9*8.

AG.text: One copy of CYP2C9*8, a slower version found mainly in people of African ancestry; see "CYP2C9 type".

AA.text: Two copies of CYP2C9*8: slower processing of warfarin, phenytoin and some NSAIDs; see "CYP2C9 type".

markers.about: A slower CYP2C9 version, one of the most common in people of African ancestry.

markers.name: CYP2C9*11

CC.text: No copies of CYP2C9*11.

CT.text: One copy of CYP2C9*11, a slower version found mainly in people of African ancestry; see "CYP2C9 type".

TT.text: Two copies of CYP2C9*11: slower processing of warfarin, phenytoin and some NSAIDs; see "CYP2C9 type".

markers.about: A slower CYP2C9 version found mainly in people of African ancestry.

markers.name: CYP2C19*4

AA.text: No copies of CYP2C19*4.

AG.text: One copy of CYP2C19*4, a less common non-working version; same cautions as CYP2C19*2. See "CYP2C19 type".

GG.text: Two copies: poor processing of some drugs, such as clopidogrel; tell prescribers.

markers.about: A less common non-working CYP2C19 version, found in about 1 in 30 Ashkenazi Jews.

markers.name: CYP2C19*8

TT.text: No copies of CYP2C19*8.

CT.text: One copy of CYP2C19*8, a less common non-working version; same cautions as CYP2C19*2. See "CYP2C19 type".

CC.text: Two copies: poor processing of some drugs, such as clopidogrel; tell prescribers.

markers.about: A less common non-working CYP2C19 version, found mainly in Europeans.

markers.name: Warfarin dose, CYP2C region (rs12777823)

GG.text: No copies of the version linked to a lower warfarin dose.

AG.text: One copy of a version that, in people of African ancestry, is linked to needing a lower warfarin dose (guidelines suggest 10 to 25% lower). It has not been shown to matter in other ancestries. Only relevant if you are prescribed warfarin.

AA.text: Two copies of a version that, in people of African ancestry, is linked to needing a lower warfarin dose (guidelines suggest 10 to 25% lower). It has not been shown to matter in other ancestries. Only relevant if you are prescribed warfarin.

markers.about: This marker near the CYP2C genes is linked to a lower warfarin dose in people of African ancestry; guidelines use it only for them.

markers.name: CYP2B6*18 (efavirenz)

TT.text: No copies of CYP2B6*18.

CT.text: One copy of CYP2B6*18, a non-working version found mainly in people of African ancestry. The HIV drug efavirenz may build up; see "CYP2B6 type".

CC.text: Two copies of CYP2B6*18: slow processing of efavirenz; guidelines recommend a lower dose. Tell prescribers.

markers.about: A non-working CYP2B6 version (the efavirenz enzyme), found mainly in people of African ancestry.

markers.name: CYP3A4*22

GG.text: No copies of CYP3A4*22.

AG.text: One copy of CYP3A4*22, which makes somewhat less of the liver enzyme that processes about half of all medicines. Effects are usually small, but levels of some drugs, such as tacrolimus, may run higher.

AA.text: Two copies of CYP3A4*22: somewhat lower CYP3A4 activity. Some drugs, such as tacrolimus, may need lower doses.

markers.caveat: Evidence for dosing changes is limited.
markers.about: CYP3A4 processes about half of all medicines. *22 lowers it somewhat; the effect is small and not yet in most guidelines.

markers.name: CYP3A5*6

CC.text: No copies of CYP3A5*6.

CT.text: One copy of CYP3A5*6, a non-working version found mainly in people of African ancestry. See "CYP3A5 type".

TT.text: Two copies of CYP3A5*6, a non-working version. See "CYP3A5 type".

markers.about: Another non-working CYP3A5 version, found mainly in people of African ancestry.

markers.name: BCHE atypical (anesthesia muscle relaxants)

TT.text: No copies of the "atypical" BCHE version.

CT.text: One copy of the atypical BCHE version. Usually no effect; the muscle relaxants succinylcholine and mivacurium, used in anesthesia, may last a little longer. Worth mentioning before surgery.

CC.text: Two copies of the atypical BCHE version: the muscle relaxants succinylcholine and mivacurium can cause paralysis lasting hours instead of minutes. Tell anesthesiologists before any surgery.

markers.caveat: Other BCHE variants are not covered.
markers.about: BCHE breaks down the anesthesia muscle relaxants succinylcholine and mivacurium. With two atypical copies their effect can last hours.

markers.name: G6PD deficiency (Mediterranean)

GG.text: No copies of the G6PD Mediterranean variant.

AG.text: One copy (X-linked) of G6PD Mediterranean, a severe form of G6PD deficiency. Women with one copy can still have some deficiency. Fava beans, some drugs (such as primaquine, dapsone and rasburicase) and some infections can trigger anemia; tell your doctor.

AA.text: G6PD Mediterranean variant present. This severe form of G6PD deficiency means fava beans, some drugs (such as primaquine, dapsone and rasburicase) and some infections can destroy red blood cells. Tell your doctors; a G6PD blood test confirms it.

markers.caveat: X-linked: males have one copy; a single variant letter in a male indicates the variant.
markers.about: The Mediterranean G6PD version is much weaker than A-, so fava beans and some drugs cause more severe anemia. Common in Mediterranean, Middle Eastern and South Asian ancestry.

markers.name: TTR V122I (heart amyloidosis)

GG.text: No copies of TTR V122I.

AG.text: One copy of TTR V122I (also called V142I), carried by about 3 to 4 in 100 people of African ancestry. It raises the risk of a stiff-heart condition (transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis) later in life, usually after 60. Many carriers never develop it. Effective treatments exist, so tell your doctor, especially if you ever have heart failure symptoms.

AA.text: Two copies of TTR V122I: a higher risk of transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis later in life. Tell your doctor; effective treatments exist.

markers.caveat: In people without African ancestry this variant is very rare, so a positive result is more likely a chip error. Confirm with a clinical test.
markers.about: TTR makes transthyretin. V122I makes it fall apart, and the pieces can stiffen the heart over decades; medicines now slow this down.

markers.name: Fatty liver, PNPLA3 I148M

CC.text: No copies of the PNPLA3 fatty-liver version.

CG.text: One copy of a common version that raises liver fat and the risk of fatty liver disease, especially with extra weight or alcohol.

GG.text: Two copies of the PNPLA3 fatty-liver version: a notably higher risk of fatty liver disease and liver scarring, especially with extra weight, diabetes or alcohol. A healthy weight and little alcohol protect the liver; ask about liver checks if you have those risk factors.

markers.about: PNPLA3 breaks down fat in liver cells. I148M is the strongest common genetic risk factor for fatty liver and scarring, and its effect grows with extra weight.

markers.name: Fatty liver, TM6SF2 E167K

CC.text: No copies of the TM6SF2 fatty-liver version.

CT.text: One copy of a version that keeps more fat in the liver, raising fatty liver risk somewhat. It also slightly lowers blood cholesterol.

TT.text: Two copies of a version that keeps more fat in the liver, raising fatty liver risk. It also lowers blood cholesterol slightly.

markers.about: TM6SF2 helps the liver export fat. This weaker version keeps more fat in the liver, while blood cholesterol runs slightly lower.

markers.name: Hemoglobin E (HBB)

CC.text: No copies of hemoglobin E.

CT.text: One copy: hemoglobin E trait. This causes no illness, but it matters for family planning: a child who inherits hemoglobin E from one parent and beta-thalassemia from the other can have a serious anemia (HbE/beta-thalassemia).

TT.text: Two copies of hemoglobin E: usually only a mild anemia with small red blood cells, which can be mistaken for iron deficiency. Confirm with a hemoglobin blood test.

markers.caveat: Most common in people of Southeast Asian ancestry. Beta-thalassemia variants are not covered.
markers.about: Hemoglobin E is very common in Southeast Asia and harmless with one copy, but with a beta-thalassemia copy it causes serious anemia.

markers.name: MEFV V726A

AA.text: No copies of the MEFV V726A variant.

AG.text: One copy of the MEFV V726A variant (familial Mediterranean fever carrier status; V726A is a milder variant). Carriers usually have no symptoms but can pass it on, which matters for family planning. Confirm clinically.

GG.text: Two copies of the MEFV V726A variant (familial Mediterranean fever; V726A is a milder variant). Two copies can mean you have the condition itself, not just carrier status. See a doctor or genetic counselor and confirm with clinical testing.

markers.caveat: Most common in people with Ashkenazi Jewish, Armenian, Arab or other Mediterranean ancestry.
markers.about: A milder MEFV variant. With another MEFV variant it can cause milder familial Mediterranean fever attacks.

markers.name: G6PC R83C

CC.text: No copies of the G6PC R83C variant.

CT.text: One copy of the G6PC R83C variant (glycogen storage disease type 1a carrier status; it affects blood sugar control during fasting). Carriers usually have no symptoms but can pass it on, which matters for family planning. Confirm clinically.

TT.text: Two copies of the G6PC R83C variant (glycogen storage disease type 1a; it affects blood sugar control during fasting). Two copies can mean you have the condition itself, not just carrier status. See a doctor or genetic counselor and confirm with clinical testing.

markers.caveat: Most common in people of Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry. Other G6PC variants are not covered.
markers.about: G6PC lets the liver release sugar between meals. Two harmful copies cause glycogen storage disease 1a; R83C is the main variant in Ashkenazi Jews.

markers.name: Kell blood group (K/k)

GG.text: Kell type k/k (K-negative), like about 91 in 100 people of European ancestry.

AG.text: Kell type K/k (K-positive). About 9 in 100 people of European ancestry are K-positive. It matters mainly for blood transfusions and pregnancy.

AA.text: Kell type K/K (K-positive), about 1 in 500 people. It matters mainly for blood transfusions.

markers.caveat: Transfusion matching uses lab typing.
markers.about: Kell is one of the most important blood groups after ABO and Rh. The K version can trigger antibodies in K-negative people after transfusion or pregnancy.

markers.name: Kidd blood group (Jka/Jkb)

GG.text: Kidd type Jk(a+b-).

AG.text: Kidd type Jk(a+b+), the most common type in people of European ancestry.

AA.text: Kidd type Jk(a-b+).

markers.caveat: Transfusion matching uses lab typing. Rare Kidd-null types are not covered.
markers.about: The Kidd blood group (Jka/Jkb) can cause delayed transfusion reactions, mainly mattering for people who need repeated transfusions.

markers.name: Lactose digestion, -13915G (Middle East)

AA.text: No copies of this lactase-persistence version, which is found mainly in people of Arabian ancestry.

AC.text: One copy of a lactase-persistence version common in people of Arabian ancestry: likely digests dairy fine as an adult.

CC.text: Two copies of a lactase-persistence version common in people of Arabian ancestry: likely digests dairy fine as an adult.

markers.about: A switch that keeps lactase on in adults; it arose separately in the Arabian Peninsula.

markers.name: Lactose digestion, -14010C (East Africa)

CC.text: No copies of this lactase-persistence version, which is found mainly in people of East African ancestry.

CG.text: One copy of a lactase-persistence version common in East Africa: likely digests dairy fine as an adult.

GG.text: Two copies of a lactase-persistence version common in East Africa: likely digests dairy fine as an adult.

markers.about: A switch that keeps lactase on in adults; it arose separately among East African herders.

markers.name: Lactose digestion, -13907G (East Africa)

GG.text: No copies of this lactase-persistence version, which is found mainly in people of East African ancestry.

CG.text: One copy of a lactase-persistence version found in East Africa: likely digests dairy fine as an adult.

CC.text: Two copies of a lactase-persistence version found in East Africa: likely digests dairy fine as an adult.

markers.about: Another East African lactase switch, found mainly in Sudan and Ethiopia.

markers.name: Eye color

AA.text: Most likely brown eyes.

AG.text: Most likely brown or hazel eyes. Green or light brown is also possible.

GG.text: Most likely light-colored eyes: blue, grey or green.

markers.caveat: This is the strongest single eye-color marker, but other genes add shades, so it is right most of the time, not always.
markers.about: This HERC2 switch controls pigment from the nearby OCA2 gene; two blue-eye copies usually give blue eyes, though other genes fine-tune the result.

markers.name: Green or hazel eyes (OCA2)

CC.text: You do not carry this eye-color modifier.

CT.text: You carry one copy of a version linked to green or hazel eyes rather than pure blue or brown, mostly in people of European ancestry.

TT.text: You carry two copies of a version linked to green or hazel eyes.

markers.caveat: A modifier: the main eye-color marker above matters more.

verify.note: Effect per Branicki 2009 / HIrisPlex.

markers.about: This OCA2 variant slightly lowers iris pigment and is linked to green and hazel eyes.

markers.name: Red hair and freckles (marker 1)

CC.text: You do not carry this red-hair version.

CT.text: You carry one copy of a red-hair version. You probably do not have red hair yourself, but you may freckle or sunburn more easily, and you could pass red hair on to your children.

TT.text: You carry two copies of a red-hair version: a good chance of red or reddish hair, freckles, and fair skin that burns easily.

markers.caveat: There are several red-hair versions of this gene; their effects add up. Marker 2 below checks another one.
markers.about: MC1R decides between dark and red pigment. R151C is a common, strongly weakening variant. Red hair usually takes two weakened MC1R copies; MC1R variants also raise skin cancer risk.

markers.name: Red hair and freckles (marker 2)

CC.text: You do not carry this second red-hair version.

CT.text: You carry one copy of a second red-hair version. On its own it mostly means more freckles and easier sunburn. If marker 1 also shows a copy, red hair is likely.

TT.text: You carry two copies of this red-hair version: a good chance of red or reddish hair and fair skin that burns easily.

markers.caveat: Use plenty of sun protection if you burn easily, whatever your result.
markers.about: MC1R decides between dark and red pigment. R160W is a common, strongly weakening variant. Red hair usually takes two weakened MC1R copies; MC1R variants also raise skin cancer risk.

markers.name: Freckles and sun sensitivity

CC.text: You do not carry the version linked to extra freckles.

CT.text: One copy of a version linked to more freckles, skin that tans less easily, and lighter hair in childhood.

TT.text: Two copies of a version linked to more freckles, skin that burns more easily, and lighter hair in childhood.

markers.caveat: Mostly seen in people with European ancestry.

verify.note: New trait marker; effect direction from published studies, needs review.

markers.about: IRF4 switches on pigment genes. This variant is linked to freckles, sun sensitivity and hair that darkens with age.

markers.name: Blond hair

TT.text: You do not carry this "blond" version.

CT.text: One copy of a version that makes hair a shade lighter. It is common in Northern Europe.

CC.text: Two copies of a version that makes hair lighter; blond hair is more likely.

markers.caveat: Hair color depends on many genes; this one has a small effect.

verify.note: New trait marker; effect direction from published studies, needs review.

markers.about: KITLG helps pigment cells work. This variant is linked to blond hair in Northern Europeans, one of many hair-color genes.

markers.name: Earwax type and body odor

CC.text: Wet earwax (sticky and honey-colored), the most common type worldwide. You likely have typical underarm odor.

CT.text: Wet earwax. You carry one copy of the dry version, but the wet version wins.

TT.text: Dry earwax (flaky and grey) and usually much less underarm odor. This is very common in people with East Asian ancestry.

markers.about: ABCC11 is a pump in sweat and earwax glands. This version gives dry earwax and less underarm odor; it is usual in East Asia and rare elsewhere.

markers.name: Muscle type ("sprinter gene")

CC.text: Your muscles make a protein (alpha-actinin-3) used in fast, powerful movements. This version is common in sprinters and power athletes.

CT.text: Your muscles make alpha-actinin-3. This is the most common result.

TT.text: Your muscles do not make alpha-actinin-3. This is harmless and common (about 1 in 5 people) and is a bit more common in endurance athletes.

markers.caveat: Training matters far more than this gene. It does not decide what sport you will be good at.
markers.about: ACTN3 is a fast-twitch muscle protein. About 1 in 5 Europeans have two copies of this variant and none of the protein, which is harmless; elite sprinters rarely do.

markers.name: Cilantro tastes like soap

CC.text: You do not carry the version linked to cilantro (coriander) tasting soapy.

AC.text: One copy of a version that slightly raises the chance cilantro tastes soapy to you.

AA.text: Two copies of that version: cilantro is more likely to taste soapy to you.

markers.caveat: A small effect. Most people with this version still like cilantro.

verify.note: New trait marker; effect direction from published studies, needs review.

markers.about: OR6A2 smells the aldehydes that make cilantro taste soapy to some. This variant explains only a small part of who dislikes it.

markers.name: How fast you process caffeine

AA.text: Fast caffeine processor: caffeine likely clears from your body quickly.

AC.text: Medium-to-slow caffeine processor: caffeine may stay in your body longer.

CC.text: Slow caffeine processor: coffee late in the day is more likely to affect your sleep.

markers.caveat: Smoking, some medicines, and pregnancy also change how fast caffeine is cleared.

verify.note: New trait marker; effect direction from published studies, needs review.

markers.about: CYP1A2 breaks down most caffeine. The fast version clears it faster when the enzyme is switched on, for example by smoking.

markers.name: Caffeine jitters

CC.text: You likely have a typical reaction to caffeine.

CT.text: You may be somewhat more likely to feel jittery from caffeine.

TT.text: You are more likely to feel anxious or jittery, or to sleep poorly, after caffeine.

markers.caveat: How much coffee you are used to drinking changes this a lot.

verify.note: New trait marker; effect direction from published studies, needs review.

markers.about: ADORA2A is the receptor caffeine blocks. This variant is linked to more anxiety and poorer sleep from caffeine.

markers.name: Skin tone gene (SLC24A5)

GG.text: Two copies of the original human version. It is most common in people with African or East Asian ancestry.

AG.text: One copy of each version.

AA.text: Two copies of a version that lightens skin. It is found in nearly everyone with European, Middle Eastern or South Asian ancestry.

markers.caveat: Skin color depends on many genes. One marker cannot tell your ancestry.
markers.about: SLC24A5 helps make melanin. This skin-lightening variant is carried by almost all Europeans and many in South Asia and the Middle East.

markers.name: Thick, straight hair gene (EDAR)

AA.text: The most common version in most of the world.

AG.text: One copy of a version linked to thicker, straighter hair and more sweat glands. It is common in people with East Asian or Native American ancestry.

GG.text: Two copies of that version. It is most common in people with East Asian or Native American ancestry.

markers.caveat: One marker cannot tell your ancestry.
markers.about: EDAR shapes hair follicles, sweat glands and teeth. This variant gives thicker hair and shovel-shaped teeth, common in East Asian and Native American ancestry.

markers.name: Malaria protection (Duffy-null)

TT.text: You do not carry the Duffy-null version.

CT.text: One copy of the Duffy-null version, which helps protect against one type of malaria. It is very common in people with African ancestry.

CC.text: Two copies (Duffy-null): your red blood cells lack the Duffy protein, which blocks one type of malaria. It is common in people with African ancestry. It also naturally lowers one white blood cell count (neutrophils) on lab tests. This is harmless, but worth telling your doctor so the result is not misread.

markers.caveat: One marker cannot tell your ancestry.
markers.about: This change switches off the Duffy protein on red cells, protecting against one malaria parasite. Usual in sub-Saharan Africa, it often comes with a harmless lower white cell count.

markers.name: Sneezing in bright sunlight

TT.text: You are less likely to sneeze when you step into bright light.

CT.text: Slightly more likely to sneeze when you step into bright light (the "photic sneeze" reflex).

CC.text: More likely to sneeze when you step into bright light.

markers.caveat: A small effect found in a large study of customers of a DNA testing company.

verify.note: New trait marker; effect direction from published studies, needs review.

markers.about: About 1 in 4 people sneeze in bright light. This variant near ZEB2 was linked to it in one large study.

markers.name: Annoyed by chewing sounds

AA.text: You are less likely to feel strong irritation at the sound of other people chewing.

AG.text: Slightly more likely to feel irritated by chewing sounds.

GG.text: More likely to feel strong irritation at the sound of other people chewing.

markers.caveat: A small effect; how you feel about it is mostly not genetic.

verify.note: New trait marker; effect direction from published studies, needs review.

markers.about: Strong irritation at chewing sounds (misophonia) was weakly linked to this TENM2 variant in one large study.

markers.name: Stomach flu (norovirus) resistance

GG.text: You can catch the most common strains of norovirus, the "stomach flu." Most people are like this.

AG.text: You can catch the most common norovirus strains. You carry one copy of the resistant version.

AA.text: You are naturally resistant to the most common norovirus ("stomach flu") strains, though not to all of them. About 1 in 5 people of European ancestry are.

markers.caveat: Good hand washing still matters; some strains can infect anyone.
markers.about: FUT2 sets "secretor" status. About 1 in 5 Europeans have two copies of this variant and are non-secretors, resistant to the most common norovirus strains.

markers.name: BRCA1 185delAG

DD.text: No copies of the BRCA1 185delAG variant.

DI.text: One copy of the BRCA1 185delAG variant (breast and ovarian cancer predisposition). This is a screening-grade result: confirm with clinical testing and talk with a doctor or genetic counselor.

II.text: Two copies of the BRCA1 185delAG variant (breast and ovarian cancer predisposition). Confirm with clinical testing and talk with a doctor or genetic counselor.

markers.caveat: Checks only 1 of thousands of BRCA variants. If family history exists, ask about clinical testing.

verify.note: Vendor letters: AncestryDNA reports the usual genotype as DD, so D = normal here even though the variant is a deletion. 23andMe reports BRCA under its own IDs. Awaiting expert review.

markers.about: Another Ashkenazi Jewish founder variant in BRCA1. It stops the protein early and carries the same high breast and ovarian cancer risk.

markers.name: HEXA 1278insTATC

DD.text: No copies of the HEXA 1278insTATC variant.

DI.text: One copy of the HEXA 1278insTATC variant (Tay-Sachs disease carrier status). Carriers usually have no symptoms but can pass it on, which matters for family planning. Confirm clinically.

II.text: Two copies of the HEXA 1278insTATC variant (Tay-Sachs disease). Two copies can mean you have the condition itself, not just carrier status. See a doctor or genetic counselor and confirm with clinical testing.

markers.caveat: Most common in people with Ashkenazi Jewish, French-Canadian or Cajun ancestry. Other HEXA variants are not covered.

verify.note: D/I: AncestryDNA reports the usual genotype as DD (D = no insertion).

markers.about: HEXA breaks down a fatty substance in nerve cells; Tay-Sachs needs both copies broken. This is the most common Tay-Sachs variant in Ashkenazi Jews.

markers.name: HEXA G269S

CC.text: No copies of the HEXA G269S variant.

CT.text: One copy of the HEXA G269S variant (late-onset Tay-Sachs disease carrier status). Carriers usually have no symptoms but can pass it on, which matters for family planning. Confirm clinically.

TT.text: Two copies of the HEXA G269S variant (late-onset Tay-Sachs disease). Two copies can mean you have the condition itself, not just carrier status. See a doctor or genetic counselor and confirm with clinical testing.

markers.caveat: Other HEXA variants are not covered.
markers.about: G269S leaves HEXA partly working. With another harmful copy it causes late-onset, milder adult Tay-Sachs.

markers.name: ASPA E285A

AA.text: No copies of the ASPA E285A variant.

AC.text: One copy of the ASPA E285A variant (Canavan disease carrier status). Carriers usually have no symptoms but can pass it on, which matters for family planning. Confirm clinically.

CC.text: Two copies of the ASPA E285A variant (Canavan disease). Two copies can mean you have the condition itself, not just carrier status. See a doctor or genetic counselor and confirm with clinical testing.

markers.caveat: Most common in people with Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry. Other ASPA variants are not covered.
markers.about: ASPA maintains the insulation around nerve fibers. Two broken copies cause Canavan disease; E285A is the most common variant in Ashkenazi Jews.

markers.name: ELP1 (IKBKAP) splice variant

AA.text: No copies of the ELP1 (IKBKAP) splice variant variant.

AG.text: One copy of the ELP1 (IKBKAP) splice variant variant (familial dysautonomia carrier status). Carriers usually have no symptoms but can pass it on, which matters for family planning. Confirm clinically.

GG.text: Two copies of the ELP1 (IKBKAP) splice variant variant (familial dysautonomia). Two copies can mean you have the condition itself, not just carrier status. See a doctor or genetic counselor and confirm with clinical testing.

markers.caveat: Most common in people with Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry.
markers.about: ELP1 is needed for nerve development. Two copies of this change cause familial dysautonomia, found almost only in Ashkenazi Jews.

markers.name: ACADM K304E

AA.text: No copies of the ACADM K304E variant.

AG.text: One copy of the ACADM K304E variant (MCAD deficiency carrier status; MCAD deficiency affects how the body uses fat for energy during fasting). Carriers usually have no symptoms but can pass it on, which matters for family planning. Confirm clinically.

GG.text: Two copies of the ACADM K304E variant (MCAD deficiency; MCAD deficiency affects how the body uses fat for energy during fasting). Two copies can mean you have the condition itself, not just carrier status. See a doctor or genetic counselor and confirm with clinical testing.

markers.caveat: Newborn screening tests for MCAD deficiency in many countries. Other ACADM variants are not covered.
markers.about: ACADM lets the body burn fat during fasting. Two harmful copies cause MCAD deficiency, which newborn screening catches and is very manageable; K304E is the most common variant.

markers.name: PAH R408W

GG.text: No copies of the PAH R408W variant.

AG.text: One copy of the PAH R408W variant (phenylketonuria (PKU) carrier status). Carriers usually have no symptoms but can pass it on, which matters for family planning. Confirm clinically.

AA.text: Two copies of the PAH R408W variant (phenylketonuria (PKU)). Two copies can mean you have the condition itself, not just carrier status. See a doctor or genetic counselor and confirm with clinical testing.

markers.caveat: Many other PAH variants exist. Newborn screening tests for PKU.
markers.about: PAH breaks down phenylalanine. Two harmful copies cause PKU, caught by newborn screening and treated by diet; R408W is the most common variant in Europeans.

markers.name: ALDOB A149P

CC.text: No copies of the ALDOB A149P variant.

CG.text: One copy of the ALDOB A149P variant (hereditary fructose intolerance carrier status; two copies mean fruit sugar can make you ill). Carriers usually have no symptoms but can pass it on, which matters for family planning. Confirm clinically.

GG.text: Two copies of the ALDOB A149P variant (hereditary fructose intolerance; two copies mean fruit sugar can make you ill). Two copies can mean you have the condition itself, not just carrier status. See a doctor or genetic counselor and confirm with clinical testing.

markers.caveat: Other ALDOB variants are not covered.
markers.about: ALDOB breaks down fructose. Two harmful copies cause hereditary fructose intolerance, managed by avoiding fructose, sugar and sorbitol.

markers.name: MEFV M694V

TT.text: No copies of the MEFV M694V variant.

CT.text: One copy of the MEFV M694V variant (familial Mediterranean fever carrier status). Carriers usually have no symptoms but can pass it on, which matters for family planning. Confirm clinically.

CC.text: Two copies of the MEFV M694V variant (familial Mediterranean fever). Two copies can mean you have the condition itself, not just carrier status. See a doctor or genetic counselor and confirm with clinical testing.
